claim: High-altitude environments require that animals meet the metabolic O2 demands for locomotion and thermogenesis in O2-thin air.
source: High-altitude environments require that animals meet the metabolic O2 demands for locomotion and thermogenesis in O2-thin air, but the degree to which convergent metabolic changes have arisen across independent high-altitude lineages or the speed at which such changes arise is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the physiological challenges of high-altitude environments, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Seven high-altitude waterfowl have inhabited the Andes at 3812–4806 m elevation over varying evolutionary time scales.
source: We examined seven high-altitude waterfowl that have inhabited the Andes (3812–4806 m elevation) over varying evolutionary time scales, to elucidate changes in biochemical pathways of energy metabolism in flight muscle relative to low-altitude sister taxa.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample characteristics.

claim: High-altitude waterfowl show increased hydroxyacyl-coA dehydrogenase activity compared to low-altitude sister taxa.
source: Convergent changes across high-altitude taxa included increased hydroxyacyl-coA dehydrogenase and succinate dehydrogenase activities, decreased lactate dehydrogenase, pyruvate kinase, creatine kinase, and cytochrome c oxidase activities, and increased myoglobin content.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental findings from the study.

claim: ATP synthase activity increased in only the longest established high-altitude taxa.
source: ATP synthase activity increased in only the longest established high-altitude taxa, whereas hexokinase activity increased in only newly established taxa.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental findings showing time-dependent changes.

claim: Hexokinase activity increased in only newly established high-altitude taxa.
source: ATP synthase activity increased in only the longest established high-altitude taxa, whereas hexokinase activity increased in only newly established taxa.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental findings showing time-dependent changes.

claim: Changes in pathways of lipid oxidation, glycolysis, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation are common strategies to cope with high-altitude hypoxia.
source: Therefore, changes in pathways of lipid oxidation, glycolysis, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation are common strategies to cope with high-altitude hypoxia, but some changes require longer evolutionary time to arise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Some metabolic changes require longer evolutionary time to arise in high-altitude waterfowl.
source: Therefore, changes in pathways of lipid oxidation, glycolysis, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation are common strategies to cope with high-altitude hypoxia, but some changes require longer evolutionary time to arise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing time-dependent changes.

claim: Flying birds at high altitude must flap their wings harder and maintain higher metabolic rates to stay aloft.
source: Flying birds face the additional challenge of maintaining lift with reductions in air density, which more than offsets the metabolic savings from reductions in drag, such that birds flying at high altitude must flap their wings harder and maintain higher metabolic rates to stay aloft (Bishop et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bishop et al., 2015.

claim: Bar-headed goose has evolutionary adaptations to high altitude including increases in effective ventilation, vital capacity and air-sac volume, haemoglobin-O2 affinity, capillarity of the flight muscle and heart, and oxidative capacity of the flight muscle.
source: In the bar-headed goose (Anser indicus), for example, evolutionary adaptations to high altitude appear to have arisen throughout the O2 transport pathway, including increases in effective ventilation, vital capacity and air-sac volume, haemoglobin-O2 affinity, capillarity of the flight muscle and heart, and oxidative capacity of the flight muscle (Jessen et al., 1991; McCracken et al., 2009a; Natarajan et al., 2015; Petschow et al., 1977; Scott et al., 2009a; Scott and Milsom, 2006; Scott and Milsom, 2007; Scott et al., 2011; Weibel, 1984; York et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Metabolic genes have been outliers in genome scans of selection in high-altitude taxa.
source: Metabolic genes have been outliers in genome scans of selection in high-altitude taxa (Qu et al., 2015), and recent studies in high-altitude populations of mice and humans point towards skeletal muscle as a common target of selection (Lundby and Calbet, 2016; Scott et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Qu et al., 2015, Lundby and Calbet, 2016, and Scott et al., 2018.

claim: Skeletal muscle is a common target of selection in high-altitude populations of mice and humans.
source: Metabolic genes have been outliers in genome scans of selection in high-altitude taxa (Qu et al., 2015), and recent studies in high-altitude populations of mice and humans point towards skeletal muscle as a common target of selection (Lundby and Calbet, 2016; Scott et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lundby and Calbet, 2016, and Scott et al., 2018.

claim: The activities of enzymes involved in energy metabolism are important determinants of capacity and flux of metabolic pathways.
source: The activities of enzymes involved in energy metabolism are important determinants of capacity and flux of metabolic pathways (Kurata et al., 2007; Madhukar et al., 2015; Vogt et al., 2002a; Vogt et al., 2002b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The maximal activities of key enzymes can be valuable markers of flux capacity.
source: Flux capacity is an emergent property of the contributions of several enzymes in a pathway that is set via hierarchical regulation, which determines the limits of metabolic fluxes that can be achieved via metabolic regulation (Suarez and Moyes, 2012), and the maximal activities of key enzymes can be valuable markers of flux capacity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Suarez and Moyes, 2012 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Some previous studies suggest that the activities of some enzymes in major energy producing pathways differ in high-altitude natives compared to their low-altitude counterparts.
source: Some previous studies suggest that the activities of some enzymes in major energy producing pathways differ in high-altitude natives compared to their low-altitude counterparts (Dawson et al., 2016; Leon-Velarde et al., 1993; Reynafarje, 1962; Rosser and Hochachka, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Similar differences in enzymatic activities have not been observed in other studies of high-altitude natives.
source: However, similar differences in enzymatic activities have not been observed in other studies of high-altitude natives (Mathieu-Costello, 2001; Scott et al., 2018), and most previous work has been limited to a small number of enzymes and/or a single or a handful of species.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mathieu-Costello, 2001 and Scott et al., 2018.

claim: The study examined variation in 13 metabolic enzymes and myoglobin content across seven species encompassing four genera of high-altitude waterfowl.
source: Here, we surveyed variation in 13 metabolic enzymes and myoglobin content across seven species encompassing four genera of high-altitude waterfowl (Family Anatidae) (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the study design and methods.

claim: The study relied primarily on paired-lineage tests to make comparisons between high- and low-altitude taxa within a phylogenetic framework.
source: We relied primarily on paired-lineage tests to make comparisons between high- and low-altitude taxa within a phylogenetic framework (Storz et al., 2010), but we also complemented these tests with standard ANOVA and phylogenetically independent contrasts (Felsenstein, 1985; Garland et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the statistical methods used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: Muscle samples were collected from 76 specimens of Anas.
source: We collected muscle samples of birds from a broad range of high-altitude sites in the Andes and from paired low-altitude sites, from species in the genera Anas (n = 76 specimens), Lophonetta (n = 21 specimens), Chloephaga (n = 20 specimens) and Oxyura (n = 16 specimens).
evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

claim: Muscle samples were collected from 21 specimens of Lophonetta.
source: We collected muscle samples of birds from a broad range of high-altitude sites in the Andes and from paired low-altitude sites, from species in the genera Anas (n = 76 specimens), Lophonetta (n = 21 specimens), Chloephaga (n = 20 specimens) and Oxyura (n = 16 specimens).
evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

claim: Andean goose has a high-altitude range of 2000–5000 m above sea level.
source: The species include strictly high-alpine specialists such as Andean goose (C. melanoptera, high-altitude range = 2000–5000 m above sea level) and puna teal (Anas puna, syn. Spatula puna, 3500–4600 m), which have diverged sufficiently from their low-altitude counterparts, Magellan goose (C. picta) and silver teal (Anas versicolor, syn. Spatula versicolor), to be classified as separate species (Fjdelsa and Krabbe, 1990).
evidence: This describes the altitude range of the species studied.

evidence: This describes the altitude range of the species studied.

Spatula cyanoptera orinomus, high-altitude range = 2500–5000 m; Anas cyanoptera, syn. Spatula cyanoptera, low-altitude resident).

claim: Yellow-billed pintail has distinct populations occupying high altitude (up to 3500–4600 m) and low altitude.
source: The yellow-billed pintail (A. georgia spinicauda) has distinct populations occupying high altitude (up to 3500–4600 m) and low altitude, but they are not considered to be separate subspecies.
evidence: This describes the altitude range and taxonomic status of the species studied.

claim: High-altitude ruddy duck has a range of 2500–4500 m.
source: Finally, we sampled a highly specialized diving duck that feeds extensively on aquatic insects, the ruddy duck, which has distinct subspecies at high altitude (O. jamaicensis ferruginea, high-altitude range = 2500–4500 m) and low altitude (O. j. jamaicensis).
evidence: This describes the altitude range of the species studied.

claim: High-altitude taxa exhibited a significant reduction in creatine kinase activity (p<0.001).
source: High-altitude taxa exhibited a significant reduction in CK activity using Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p<0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: There was a significant main effect of altitude on creatine kinase activity (p<0.0001).
source: There was also a significant main effect of altitude (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b) using two-factor ANOVA and a negative correlation between CK activity and altitude using phylogenetically independent contrasts (PICs) (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: There was a negative correlation between creatine kinase activity and altitude using phylogenetically independent contrasts (p<0.0001).
source: There was also a significant main effect of altitude (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b) using two-factor ANOVA and a negative correlation between CK activity and altitude using phylogenetically independent contrasts (PICs) (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Reductions in creatine kinase activity could be a plastic response to chronic hypoxia, as observed in humans exposed to high altitude.
source: These changes could have been a plastic response to chronic hypoxia, as observed in humans exposed to high altitude (Levett et al., 2015; Viganò et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to studies in humans.

claim: Most of the creatine kinase in muscle is cytosolic.
source: Since most of the CK in muscle is cytosolic, reductions in CK activity likely reflect a reduction in cytosolic ATP buffering capacity and/or a shift towards a more oxidative phenotype.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about creatine kinase localization.

claim: Reductions in creatine kinase activity likely reflect a reduction in cytosolic ATP buffering capacity and/or a shift towards a more oxidative phenotype.
source: Since most of the CK in muscle is cytosolic, reductions in CK activity likely reflect a reduction in cytosolic ATP buffering capacity and/or a shift towards a more oxidative phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed reduction in CK activity.

claim: The activity of the phosphocreatine shuttle is augmented in high-altitude bar-headed geese.
source: However, the activity of the phosphocreatine shuttle is augmented, not reduced, in high-altitude bar-headed geese, and mitochondrial CK expression is elevated in high-altitude deer mice (Lui et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2009b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lui et al., 2015 and Scott et al., 2009b.

claim: Mitochondrial creatine kinase expression is elevated in high-altitude deer mice.
source: However, the activity of the phosphocreatine shuttle is augmented, not reduced, in high-altitude bar-headed geese, and mitochondrial CK expression is elevated in high-altitude deer mice (Lui et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2009b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lui et al., 2015 and Scott et al., 2009b.

claim: Decreases in creatine kinase activity may be part of a general strategy to down-regulate some contributors to substrate-level phosphorylation in the muscle of high-altitude waterfowl.
source: These results suggest that decreases in CK activity, along with reductions in LDH and PK activities, may be part of a general strategy to down-regulate some contributors to substrate-level phosphorylation in the muscle of high-altitude waterfowl.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns of enzyme activity changes.

claim: Hexokinase activity was elevated in some of the least established high-altitude taxa.
source: However, hexokinase (HK) activity was elevated in some of the least established high-altitude taxa (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 1f), so the decreases in LDH and PK activities are not associated with general reductions in capacity across glycolysis.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1f.

claim: HOAD activity was significantly elevated in highland taxa using Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (p<0.001).
source: HOAD activity was significantly elevated in highland taxa using Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (p<0.001; Figure 3), and there was a significant main effect of altitude using two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b) and a positive correlation between HOAD activity and altitude using PIC (p=0.0001; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: There was a significant main effect of altitude on HOAD activity using two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001).
source: HOAD activity was significantly elevated in highland taxa using Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (p<0.001; Figure 3), and there was a significant main effect of altitude using two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b) and a positive correlation between HOAD activity and altitude using PIC (p=0.0001; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: There was a positive correlation between HOAD activity and altitude using phylogenetically independent contrasts (p=0.0001).
source: HOAD activity was significantly elevated in highland taxa using Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (p<0.001; Figure 3), and there was a significant main effect of altitude using two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b) and a positive correlation between HOAD activity and altitude using PIC (p=0.0001; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors are key regulators of the expression of genes encoding the mitochondrial trifunctional enzyme and other enzymes in beta-oxidation.
source: The peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPAR) are key regulators of the expression of genes encoding the mitochondrial trifunctional enzyme (the heterooctamer that catalyzes the HOAD step and two additional steps in beta-oxidation) and other enzymes in beta-oxidation (i.e., acyl-CoA dehydrogenases), as well as genes controlling fatty-acid transport into mitochondria (Fan and Evans, 2015), so increases in HOAD activity in the flight muscle could reflect a general increase in the capacity for lipid oxidation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fan and Evans, 2015.

claim: Increases in HOAD activity in the flight muscle could reflect a general increase in the capacity for lipid oxidation.
source: The peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPAR) are key regulators of the expression of genes encoding the mitochondrial trifunctional enzyme (the heterooctamer that catalyzes the HOAD step and two additional steps in beta-oxidation) and other enzymes in beta-oxidation (i.e., acyl-CoA dehydrogenases), as well as genes controlling fatty-acid transport into mitochondria (Fan and Evans, 2015), so increases in HOAD activity in the flight muscle could reflect a general increase in the capacity for lipid oxidation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increase in HOAD activity.

claim: Fatty-acid oxidation is strongly regulated by the enzymes involved in mitochondrial lipid uptake.
source: However, fatty-acid oxidation is strongly regulated by the enzymes involved in mitochondrial lipid uptake (e.g., carnitine palmitoyl transferase), such that changes in fatty acid oxidation can arise without changes in HOAD activity (Morash et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Morash et al., 2013.

claim: Birds have a remarkable capacity to support high rates of muscle metabolism and power on lipids alone.
source: Nevertheless, if increases in HOAD activity are indeed associated with increased capacity for lipid oxidation in the flight muscle, such changes would amplify the already remarkable capacity of birds to support high rates of muscle metabolism and power on lipids alone (Guglielmo, 2010; O'Brien and Suarez, 2001; Suarez et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Guglielmo, 2010, O'Brien and Suarez, 2001, and Suarez et al., 1986.

claim: Sustained thermogenesis relies heavily on lipid oxidation.
source: Sustained thermogenesis relies heavily on lipid oxidation (Marsh and Dawson, 1989; Swanson and Thomas, 2007; Vaillancourt et al., 2009; Vaillancourt et al., 2005), such that cold temperatures could have increased lipid metabolism and stimulated a corresponding rise in beta-oxidation capacity in high-altitude birds.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cold temperatures could have increased lipid metabolism and stimulated a corresponding rise in beta-oxidation capacity in high-altitude birds.
source: Sustained thermogenesis relies heavily on lipid oxidation (Marsh and Dawson, 1989; Swanson and Thomas, 2007; Vaillancourt et al., 2009; Vaillancourt et al., 2005), such that cold temperatures could have increased lipid metabolism and stimulated a corresponding rise in beta-oxidation capacity in high-altitude birds.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism for increased beta-oxidation capacity.

claim: There is a positive association between altitude and body lipid content in insects.
source: Furthermore, there seems to be a positive association between altitude and body lipid content in insects (Parkash et al., 2008; Sømme et al., 1996), which could increase dietary lipid availability at high altitude for waterfowl (most of which forage on aquatic insects).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Parkash et al., 2008 and Sømme et al., 1996.

claim: There is a positive correlation between dietary lipids and HOAD activity in the pectoralis of both migratory and non-migratory birds.
source: There is also evidence showing a positive correlation between dietary lipids and HOAD activity in the pectoralis of both migratory and non-migratory birds (Guglielmo, 2010; Maillet and Weber, 2007; Nagahuedi et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

claim: Cytochrome c oxidase had approximately 50% lower activity in high-altitude species compared to low-altitude sister taxa across nearly all high-altitude species except the ruddy duck.
source: In contrast, the terminal acceptor for oxygen, cytochrome c oxidase (COX; complex IV), had ~50% lower activity when compared to low-altitude sister taxa across nearly all high-altitude species except the ruddy duck.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

claim: All high-altitude species converged on a strikingly similar value for cytochrome c oxidase activity.
source: In fact, there seemed to be a narrow optimum for the activity of COX across high-altitude waterfowl, as all species converged on a strikingly similar value (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: There was a significant main effect of altitude on COX activity in two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001).
source: COX activity showed a significant reduction in highland taxa using Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (p<0.05; Figure 3), and there was a significant main effect of altitude in two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b) and a negative correlation between COX activity and altitude using PIC (p=0.0001; Supplementary file 1f).

evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Unique specializations in the activity, structure and function of COX have been observed in the locomotory muscles of several high-altitude taxa.
source: Unique specializations in the activity, structure and function of COX have been observed in the locomotory muscles of several high-altitude taxa (Dawson et al., 2016; Lui et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2011; Sheafor, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A similar reduction in COX activity (~50% less) was observed in the cardiac muscle of bar-headed goose compared to low-altitude geese, in association with an increased affinity for cytochrome c.

claim: COX of some hypoxia-tolerant fish has decreased activity but a greater affinity for O2.

claim: Hypoxia may drive convergent changes in COX and mitochondrial function across vertebrates.

evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: The effect of altitude on myoglobin content was nearly significant in Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (0.1 > P > 0.05).
source: Myoglobin content showed a significant main effect of altitude (p=0.0077; Supplementary file 1b) using two-factor ANOVA and this effect was nearly significant in Wilcoxon's signed-rank test (0.1 > P > 0.05; Figure 5B) and in PIC correlations between myoglobin content and altitude (p=0.0706; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: The correlation between myoglobin content and altitude was nearly significant in PIC analysis (p=0.0706).

claim: Myoglobin content was variable across species and tended to be greatest in ducks with the highest body mass.
source: Myoglobin content was variable across species and tended to be greatest in ducks with the highest body mass (Supplementary file 1a), and the effect of body mass was nearly significant (p=0.0585; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental observations from the study.

claim: The effect of body mass on myoglobin content was nearly significant (p=0.0585).
source: Myoglobin content was variable across species and tended to be greatest in ducks with the highest body mass (Supplementary file 1a), and the effect of body mass was nearly significant (p=0.0585; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Body mass was not significantly greater in high-altitude waterfowl (p=0.9707).
source: Body mass, however, was not significantly greater in high-altitude waterfowl (p=0.9707; Supplementary file 1b), suggesting that the elevated levels of myoglobin in some high-altitude taxa is not simply due to increased body size.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: The elevated levels of myoglobin in some high-altitude taxa is not simply due to increased body size.
source: Body mass, however, was not significantly greater in high-altitude waterfowl (p=0.9707; Supplementary file 1b), suggesting that the elevated levels of myoglobin in some high-altitude taxa is not simply due to increased body size.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of significant difference in body mass.

claim: Elevated myoglobin content in flight muscle may serve to increase cellular O2 stores and to facilitate intracellular O2 diffusion.
source: Elevated myoglobin content in flight muscle may serve to increase cellular O2 stores and to facilitate intracellular O2 diffusion (Kanatous et al., 2009; Wittenberg and Wittenberg, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kanatous et al., 2009 and Wittenberg and Wittenberg, 2003.

claim: Elevated myoglobin content could potentially augment intracellular lipid transport as well.
source: Elevated myoglobin content could potentially augment intracellular lipid transport as well, as there are some suggestions that myoglobin may bind and facilitate fatty acid diffusion through the sarcoplasm (Gros et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Gros et al., 2010.

claim: Elevated myoglobin content or transcript expression has been previously observed in some other taxa that reside at and/or were acclimatized to high altitude, including torrent ducks, dogs, rats, and Tibetan humans.
source: Elevated myoglobin content or transcript expression has been previously observed in some other taxa that reside at and/or were acclimatized to high altitude, including torrent ducks (Mergantta armata) (Dawson et al., 2016), dogs (Gimenez et al., 1977), rats (Vaughan and Pace, 1956), and Tibetan humans (Moore et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Elevated myoglobin levels in the locomotory muscle appear to be an important strategy across high-altitude taxa for augmenting mitochondrial O2 availability and sustaining thermogenesis and locomotion in hypoxia at high altitude.
source: Therefore, elevated myoglobin levels in the locomotory muscle appear to be an important strategy across high-altitude taxa for augmenting mitochondrial O2 availability (and possibly intracellular lipid transport) and thus sustaining thermogenesis and locomotion in hypoxia at high altitude.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns across multiple taxa.

claim: Low-altitude ruddy ducks have relatively high activities of HOAD, complex II, and HK compared to other low-altitude taxa in this study.
source: Low-altitude ruddy ducks seem to have fundamentally different physiological and biochemical characteristics than the other low-altitude taxa in this study, with relatively high activities of HOAD, complex II, and HK, relatively low activities of complex IV (Figures 3–6), and a relatively high haemoglobin-O2 affinity atypical of low-altitude populations but more similar to high-altitude waterfowl populations (Natarajan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental observations from the study.

claim: Low-altitude ruddy ducks have relatively low activities of complex IV compared to other low-altitude taxa in this study.
source: Low-altitude ruddy ducks seem to have fundamentally different physiological and biochemical characteristics than the other low-altitude taxa in this study, with relatively high activities of HOAD, complex II, and HK, relatively low activities of complex IV (Figures 3–6), and a relatively high haemoglobin-O2 affinity atypical of low-altitude populations but more similar to high-altitude waterfowl populations (Natarajan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental observations from the study.

claim: Low-altitude ruddy ducks have a relatively high haemoglobin-O2 affinity atypical of low-altitude populations but more similar to high-altitude waterfowl populations.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Natarajan et al., 2015.

claim: High-altitude ruddy ducks had decreased activities of both complex II and HOAD in the flight muscle compared to low-altitude ruddy ducks.
source: Compared to this low-altitude relative, high-altitude ruddy ducks had decreased activities of both complex II and HOAD in the flight muscle, in contrast to most/all other high-altitude taxa in which the activities of these enzymes were elevated (Figure 3C; Figure 4A), and they also do not show the typical and expected increase in Hb-O2 affinity that is seen in the other high-altitude waterfowl from this study system (Natarajan et al., 2015) and in many other high-altitude birds (Storz, 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental observations from the study.

claim: High-altitude ruddy ducks do not show the typical increase in Hb-O2 affinity that is seen in other high-altitude waterfowl.
source: Compared to this low-altitude relative, high-altitude ruddy ducks had decreased activities of both complex II and HOAD in the flight muscle, in contrast to most/all other high-altitude taxa in which the activities of these enzymes were elevated (Figure 3C; Figure 4A), and they also do not show the typical and expected increase in Hb-O2 affinity that is seen in the other high-altitude waterfowl from this study system (Natarajan et al., 2015) and in many other high-altitude birds (Storz, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Natarajan et al., 2015 and Storz, 2016.

claim: The distinct direction of the differences between high- and low-altitude ruddy ducks contributed to significant species × altitude interactions for PK, HOAD, complex II, and complex IV activities.
source: The distinct direction of the differences between high- and low-altitude ruddy ducks appeared to strongly contribute to the significant species × altitude interactions that were detected in two-factor ANOVAs for PK (p=0.0003), HOAD (p<0.0001), complex II (p<0.0001), and complex IV (p<0. 001) activities (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Diving created a unique set of physiological challenges for ruddy ducks as they invaded high-altitude habitats.
source: It is possible that diving created a unique set of physiological challenges for this species as it invaded high-altitude habitats; however, we do not see similar changes in enzyme activities in the pectoralis (flight muscle) or gastrocnemius (swimming muscle) of torrent ducks at high altitude, another diving duck species native to the Andes (Dawson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement that is countered by evidence from torrent ducks.

claim: The unique features of low-altitude ruddy ducks favoured distinct mechanisms of adaptation or plasticity during the process of high-altitude colonization.
source: It is more likely that the unique features of low-altitude ruddy ducks – related to diet, physiology, biochemistry, etc. – favoured distinct mechanisms of adaptation or plasticity during the process of high-altitude colonization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns in ruddy ducks.

claim: The high-altitude taxa studied most likely diverged from their low-altitude sister taxa for evolutionary times that differed by as much as three orders of magnitude.
source: Using population genetic data for the mtDNA control region, we determined that the high-altitude taxa studied here most likely diverged from their low-altitude sister taxa for evolutionary times that differed by as much as three orders of magnitude, from within the last several thousands of years (i.e., more recently established high-altitude populations) to approximately a million years in the case of species that are now established high-altitude endemic species (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of results from population genetic analysis.

claim: In each case, all available evidence indicates that high-altitude taxa were derived from low-altitude ancestral populations and not the reverse.
source: In each case, all available evidence indicates that high-altitude taxa were derived from low-altitude ancestral populations and not the reverse (Bulgarella et al., 2014; Bulgarella et al., 2012; Fjeldså, 1985; Graham et al., 2018; McCracken et al., 2009b; McCracken et al., 2009c; Muñoz-Fuentes et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ATP synthase activity was elevated in only the most established high-altitude taxa.

evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: No differences in ATP synthase activity were observed in the newly established high-altitude populations.
source: Following this classification, ATP synthase activity was elevated in only the most established high-altitude taxa, whereas no differences were observed in the newly established populations (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The magnitude of increases in ATP synthase activity in established high-altitude taxa ranged from 2.0- to 3.1-fold.
source: The magnitude of these increases in established high-altitude taxa were appreciable, ranging from 2.0- to 3.1-fold, and they appeared to strongly contribute to the significant species × altitude interaction that was detected in two-factor ANOVA (p=0.0342; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

claim: Increases in ATP synthase activity contributed to a significant species × altitude interaction in two-factor ANOVA (p=0.0342).
source: The magnitude of these increases in established high-altitude taxa were appreciable, ranging from 2.0- to 3.1-fold, and they appeared to strongly contribute to the significant species × altitude interaction that was detected in two-factor ANOVA (p=0.0342; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Increases in ATP synthesis capacity could reduce mitochondrial membrane potential and attenuate the production of reactive oxygen species.
source: These changes would have led to a strong increase in the capacity for ATP synthesis relative to electron transport. Such a change could reduce mitochondrial membrane potential and attenuate the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which may be advantageous at high altitude for reducing oxidative stress (Brand et al., 1999; Korshunov et al., 1997; Skulachev, 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to Brand et al., 1999, Korshunov et al., 1997, and Skulachev, 1996.

claim: Increasing ATP synthesis capacity may reduce the magnitude of phosphorylation control over mitochondrial respiration.
source: Increasing ATP synthesis capacity may also reduce the magnitude of phosphorylation control over mitochondrial respiration, shifting more control towards the electron transport system (Gnaiger et al., 2000; Jacobs et al., 2012; Pesta and Gnaiger, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gnaiger et al., 2000, Jacobs et al., 2012, and Pesta and Gnaiger, 2012.

claim: Newly established populations at high altitude show increased HK activity in comparison to low-altitude populations.
source: Our results also show that newly established populations at high altitude show increased HK activity in comparison to low-altitude populations (Figure 3D; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results shown in Figures 3D and 6C,D.

claim: Only newly established and intermediate high-altitude populations had elevated HK activities, ranging from 2.20- to 3.56-fold.
source: Only newly established and intermediate high-altitude populations had elevated HK activities, ranging from 2.20- to 3.56-fold, which likely contributed to the significant species × altitude interaction that was detected in two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

claim: Elevated HK activities contributed to a significant species × altitude interaction in two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001).
source: Only newly established and intermediate high-altitude populations had elevated HK activities, ranging from 2.20- to 3.56-fold, which likely contributed to the significant species × altitude interaction that was detected in two-factor ANOVA (p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the study.

claim: Hypoxia exposure can lead to plastic increases in the reliance on carbohydrate oxidation in mammals.
source: Hypoxia exposure can lead to plastic increases in the reliance on carbohydrate oxidation in mammals (Hochachka et al., 1998; McClelland et al., 1998; Robin et al., 1984) and may be useful at high altitude by generating more ATP per molecule of O2 than lipid oxidation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hochachka et al., 1998, McClelland et al., 1998, and Robin et al., 1984.

claim: Carbohydrate oxidation may be useful at high altitude by generating more ATP per molecule of O2 than lipid oxidation.
source: Hypoxia exposure can lead to plastic increases in the reliance on carbohydrate oxidation in mammals (Hochachka et al., 1998; McClelland et al., 1998; Robin et al., 1984) and may be useful at high altitude by generating more ATP per molecule of O2 than lipid oxidation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about metabolic efficiency.

claim: Carbohydrate oxidation may be constrained over time by glycogen stores if carbohydrate fuels cannot be adequately supplied by the circulation.
source: However, carbohydrate oxidation may be constrained over time by glycogen stores if carbohydrate fuels cannot be adequately supplied by the circulation (McClelland, 2004), and we observed that the rise in HK activity in newly-established populations returned to low-altitude levels in the most established high-altitude taxa (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McClelland, 2004.

claim: The rise in HK activity in newly-established populations returned to low-altitude levels in the most established high-altitude taxa.
source: However, carbohydrate oxidation may be constrained over time by glycogen stores if carbohydrate fuels cannot be adequately supplied by the circulation (McClelland, 2004), and we observed that the rise in HK activity in newly-established populations returned to low-altitude levels in the most established high-altitude taxa (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: High-altitude animals rely upon hypoxia acclimatization when first colonising high altitude.
source: It is likely that high-altitude animals rely upon hypoxia acclimatization (Hochachka et al., 1998) when first colonising high altitude, followed by evolved physiological specializations that adjust the capacity and flux of metabolic pathways, along with evolved improvements in mitochondrial O2 supply that arise from increases in tissue capillarity (Leon-Velarde et al., 1993; Mathieu-Costello et al., 1998; Scott et al., 2009a), Hb-O2 affinity (Galen et al., 2015; Natarajan et al., 2015; Projecto-Garcia et al., 2013), circulatory O2 delivery, and/or pulmonary O2 uptake (Calbet et al., 2003; Maina et al., 2017; McClelland and Scott, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Increases in capacity for beta oxidation, changes in capacity across glycolysis, and adjustments in mitochondrial function are common strategies to cope with the challenges of high altitudes.
source: Our data suggest that increases in capacity for beta oxidation, changes in capacity across glycolysis, and adjustments in mitochondrial function are common strategies to cope with the challenges of high altitudes, but that longer time scales of evolutionary adaptation can be required to fully converge upon the ultimate high-altitude phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Longer time scales of evolutionary adaptation can be required to fully converge upon the ultimate high-altitude phenotype.
source: Our data suggest that increases in capacity for beta oxidation, changes in capacity across glycolysis, and adjustments in mitochondrial function are common strategies to cope with the challenges of high altitudes, but that longer time scales of evolutionary adaptation can be required to fully converge upon the ultimate high-altitude phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing time-dependent changes.

claim: Citrate synthase is a common marker of mitochondrial volume density in muscle tissue.
source: Citrate synthase in particular is a common marker of mitochondrial volume density in muscle tissue (Boushel et al., 2007; Dawson et al., 2018; Larsen et al., 2016; Mahalingam et al., 2017; Mogensen et al., 2006), so this result suggests that muscle mitochondrial content was similar between high- and low-altitude populations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Muscle mitochondrial content was similar between high- and low-altitude populations.
source: Citrate synthase in particular is a common marker of mitochondrial volume density in muscle tissue (Boushel et al., 2007; Dawson et al., 2018; Larsen et al., 2016; Mahalingam et al., 2017; Mogensen et al., 2006), so this result suggests that muscle mitochondrial content was similar between high- and low-altitude populations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of change in citrate synthase activity.

claim: The observed changes in complexes II, IV, and V activities could reflect a change in mitochondrial quality affecting the function of a given amount of mitochondria.
source: The observed changes in complexes II, IV, and V activities could therefore reflect a change in mitochondrial quality affecting the function of a given amount of mitochondria.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed enzyme activity changes in the context of unchanged citrate synthase activity.

claim: Flight muscle tends to become more oxidative at deeper depths from the ventral surface.
source: This heterogeneity is important to consider, because flight muscle tends to become more oxidative at deeper depths from the ventral surface (Scott et al., 2009a), as confirmed by the variation observed here (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Scott et al., 2009a and confirmed by data in the study.

claim: The Andes have been rising throughout the Cenozoic for approximately 80 million years.
source: Finally, it should be noted that the Andes have been rising throughout the Cenozoic for approximately 80 million years (Ramos, 2005; Royden et al., 2008), and while some parts of the Andes uplifted more recently than others, the oldest of these waterfowl populations (i.e., South American sheldgeese) are probably diverged no more than several millions years ago (Johnson and Sorenson, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ramos, 2005 and Royden et al., 2008.

claim: The oldest of the waterfowl populations studied are probably diverged no more than several millions years ago.
source: Finally, it should be noted that the Andes have been rising throughout the Cenozoic for approximately 80 million years (Ramos, 2005; Royden et al., 2008), and while some parts of the Andes uplifted more recently than others, the oldest of these waterfowl populations (i.e., South American sheldgeese) are probably diverged no more than several millions years ago (Johnson and Sorenson, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Johnson and Sorenson, 1999.

claim: In all cases the Andes had already uplifted to close to their present height when these high-altitude populations first became established.
source: Therefore, in all cases the Andes had already uplifted to close to their present height when these high-altitude populations first became established.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the geological history of the Andes and the divergence times of the waterfowl populations.

claim: All TCA cycle enzymes assayed, including citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase, were similar between high- and low-altitude populations.
source: The activities of all TCA cycle enzymes assayed, including citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase, were similar between high- and low-altitude populations (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

source: The maximal activities of 13 enzymes as well as myoglobin content were assayed as previously described (Dawson et al., 2016) using a Spectramax Plus 384 spectrophotomer (Molecular Devices, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) at avian body temperature of 41°C.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.
